Mr. Speaker, yesterday the
hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) asked a question respecting the Italian duty on salt fish, and I should like to make the following answer:
Dried codfish, of which exports to Italy were about one-half million dollars in each of the calendar years 1933 and 1934, had been entering Italy free of duty up to September 24, 1931. On that date a special new duty of 15 per cent ad valorem was introduced and applied to imports in general, including codfish. There has been no change in the Italian tariff on codfish since that date.
An Italian royal decree law, effective on February 19, 1935, instituted an import licence system affecting practically all imports into Italy. The purpose of the system was officially

British Columbia Relief Camps
stated to be the maintenance of the value of Italian currency by reducing a rising adverse trade balance.
Import control is exercised by allowing the importation of fixed percentages of what was imported during the corresponding period in the year 1934. The percentage limits vary for different products and range from 10 per cent to 35 per cent, the percentage for codfish being fixed at 20 per cent. The quotas are fixed with reference to total imports into Italy, regardless of the country of origin and without discrimination against any particular supplying country. There is a provision, however, that imports may be increased from countries which agree to purchase Italian exports either by means of clearing agreements between the exporting country and Italy or by barter agreements between individual Italian and foreign firms.
Provision is further made for modifying these quota restrictions by means of trade agreements effected between Italy and other countries. In such case a larger quota may be allotted for the country concluding an agreement with Italy based also on a percentage of previous total imports. Shortly after the Italian quota restrictions came into force steps were taken to enter into negotiations with Italy for the conclusion of an agreement which would result in larger quotas being accorded to Canadian products. In this regard an offer has been submitted to Italy and we are now awaiting the outcome of the discussions which have taken place.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STRIKE OF WORKERS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA- STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the hon. gentleman had been good enough to give me some intimation that he proposed to ask the question I would have brought with me papers that would have enabled me to deal with the matter in more detail. I shall be glad, however, to make a statement now subject to any corrections that may be necessary, relying entirely as I do upon my memory for the present statement.
In the early part of this year, as well as last year, representations were made by the provinces that they were unable to care for their unemployed without assistance from the federal government. The federal government did make contributions in money to enable the provinces to care for the unemployed, as is their constitutional duty.
Another question, however, arose with respect to transients, single unemployed men, and with respect to them the provinces other than Prince Edward Island urged that steps be taken by the federal government to provide entirely, so long as they remained in the camps, for the upkeep of these men-. The federal government acceded to that request and camps were established in every one of the provinces except Prince Edward Island for single unemployed men. These men were supplied with food, with shelter, with clothing, and a small per diem allowance for incidentals. There has been no trouble of any importance in any of the provinces except British Columbia.
The conditions under which these camps were maintained were three : First, that there should be the power of rejection with respect to applicants who were known to be of a troublesome character and whose introduction into the camps was solely for the purpose of making trouble. Secondly, there were no disciplinary measures contemplated or provided for. Thirdly, whenever an opportunity for work offered, any person who was in these camps might avail himself of that opportunity for work. In addition to that steps were taken where regular employment was offering to point out to those in the camps that the opportunity was afforded to them to find employment.
Last year the premier of British Columbia and his attorney general represented to this

British Columbia Relief Camps
government that they were experiencing great difficulties in connection with logging operations in that province through the activities of agitating communists. They had no hesitation in saying that that was so. In the month of April this year we were advised that a strike might be imminent in the camps in British Columbia, and the British Columbia authorities were advised accordingly. Might I state here what must be known to every member of this house, that the federal government under our constitution cannot take any steps towards the preservation of law and order or the administration of criminal law in any province of this confederation except at the request of the provincial authorities. We therefore cannot do any legal act with respect to those who are themselves engaged in illegal transactions except such action be taken at the request of the province.
Owing to the agitation that took place, owing to the action of the agitators in the camps of British Columbia, large numbers of the men left their camps and went into the city of Vancouver. The result was that there was a large number of unemployed single men from these camps who claimed that the province should supply them with sustenance. The province, of course, could very properly reply that they did have sustenance provided for them in the camps, but the men would not go back to the camps and have not gone back to them. In the meantime, for reasons that are best known to themselves, the provincial authorities have intimated that a duty was cast upon the federal government to expand its currency by a species of inflation and provide work and wages in that manner for those who had left the camps and gone to the city.
I have not yet sent a communication to the premier of British Columbia except in general terms when last night a message was dispatched to the mayor of Vancouver and a copy sent to him, for there is no medium of contact between the municipalities and the dominion with respect to matters of law and order. The province, and the province alone, is the competent authority with which the dominion deals, and can only deal so far as our constitution is concerned until it is amended from its present form. I have drafted a communication to the premier of British Columbia in which I have endeavoured to point out that if the province fails in its duty to prevent a condition of chaos and anarchy arising, if they fail in their duty to maintain law and order in the province of British Columbia, it will only be because they have not availed themselves of

the opportunity of requesting the federal government to lend them such assistance as may be required for that purpose, for until that is done any action on the part of this dominion would be wholly illegal and would be a compromising of our own position with those who may themselves be violating the law. Ever since there was the first intimation that in the province of British Columbia there was dissatisfaction it has always been maintained by the federal government that they are ready and prepared to discuss with the provincial government the situation in all its details. We have again repeated that position. But I do assert, and I believe I represent the considered opinion of every thoughtful man in this dominion, that as long as there are incentives being given to men to maintain a chaotic and anarchic condition in the city of Vancouver or elsewhere in the province of British Columbia, there can be no adjustment of differences or difficulties. The differences and difficulties, whatever they may be, the federal government will be glad to consider with the provincial government, but it is a condition precedent to any such action that law and order be maintained by those who are responsible for it, and if they are unable to do so that they call upon the federal government for such assistance as will enable them to do so. There can be no trifling with anarchy, there can be no playing with chaos, and so far as this government is concerned it proposes within the ambit of its power to be always ready and willing to assist those who are charged with that responsibility if they find themselves unable so to do themselves. But mob violence, mob threats, mob law will not be the means by which to deal with matters of this kind between the province of British Columbia and the Dominion of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I wish to bring up a question of privilege in regard to a press dispatch which appeared in the Ottawa newspapers of yesterday afternoon, amid which was brought to my attention by friends last night, in which a charge is mode, among other things, that the Minister of Justice was guilty of a gross breach of faith ini regard to an incident described in the newspaper article. The dispatch comes from Toronto, dated May 20, and is as follows:
Toronto, May 20.-(C.P.)-Hon. A. W. Roebuck, Ontario attorney-general, to-day started his inquiry into the case of Aemilius Jarvis, former Toronto broker, to determine if he will recommend to Hon. Hugh Guthrie, federal Minister of Justice, that Jarvis be granted a new trial.
In October, 1924, Jarvis, along with the late Peter Smith, provincial treasurer in the former Drury government, was convicted on a conspiracy charge. Smith was sentenced to three years in penitentiary and a joint fine of $600,000 with Jarvis. Jarvis was sent to county jail for six months. On appealing his sentence Jarvis' fine was reduced to $60,000 and in addition he was forced to make restitution of $140,000 profit allegedly made on a bond deal with the Ontario government.
Efforts to obtain a new trial were unsuccessful. When he renewed his plea, the government of Premier Hepburn instructed Mr. Roebuck to inquire into the case.
Criticism was voiced by Mr. Sedgwick, of the Ontario attorney-general's department against the Minister of Justice for turning over to Jarvis' lawyers "a private and confidential document" prepared by the attorney-general's department on the case after petitions had been presented to the federal minister asking a new trial.
"Unless I am mistaken, it is a gross breach of faith to hand over a private and confidential document to the party about whom it is written," declared Mr. Sedgwick.
"If the attorney-general's statements in the document are true, I don't see why it should be private and confidential," retorted Mr. Hayden.
"We are not trying the good faith of the minister at Ottawa," Mr. Roebuck interjected.
Two of my friends last night informed me that the amticle specifically charged me with being guilty .of a gross breach .of faith, and I have no doubt the public may consider it as a direct reference to myself-and as this dispatch has received very wide circulation throughout the province, of Ontario and probably throughout .the Dominion of Canada, I desire to enter a formal denial.
The incident referred to in this article* occurred in the month of December, 1928, nearly two years before I became Minister of 92582-186
Justice; but while speaking in my own defence, I think I may also join with myself my predecessor in that office and speak for him as well, because there is no foundation in fact, and nothing in the circumstances, to warrant such a statement being made by an official of (the Attorney General's department in Toronto either against myself or my predecessor. The incident was simply this. In 1928 application was made to my predecessor for .a new trial, and a communication' had been received by the Minister of Justice from the Attorney General' of Ontario in regard to the Jarvis case. Jarvis was represented, in the application for a new trial, by Mr. Aime Geoffriom, K.C., and Mr. A. G. Slaght, K.C., of Toronto. They asked- to see the communication received by the Minister of Justice from the Attorney General of Ontario, but as -is the rule in the department, all such communications -are considered private and privileged and they were informed that the document could not be handed to them. However, they said .that .they would like to see it in1 order .that they might be able to answer it, and the Minister .of Justice, the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe), instructed an official -of the department to communicate with the Attorney General of Ontario 'and obtain his view on the matter, as to whether the document should be handed over or not. Accordingly, on December 13, 1928, a .telegram was sent to thie Attorney General of Ontario by M. F. Gallagher of the remissions branch, which deals with questions of this kind. A reply was received the following day. While I have not the reply before me, I have the letter confirming it and I will* read it .to ithe house. It is dajted Toronto, December 15, 1928, and reads:

M. F. Gallagher, Esq.,
Chief of the Remissions Branch,
Department of Justice,

speechtext:
When the house rose last night, I was answering some of the criticisms that .had been made of the attitude of hon. gentlemen on this side in regard to this bill. Since that time I have had an opoprtunity of seeing the order in council that was passed in 1913. One of the claims made and urged very strongly by my hon. friends opposite was that this was a compliance with an agreement that had been entered into at that time. I do not know that that is an altogether incorrect statement, but may I point out that so far as I am able to ascertain, no agreement was ever entered into between the government and the harbour commission. What took place was that an order in council was passed providing for the expenditure by the government of an amount that /was then estimated, including the bridges that have been referred to in this discussion, at $6,400,000. As regards the bascule bridge as a substitute for which the tunnel is now proposed, the estimate for that bridge has been referred to by some hon. gentlemen opposite as being $800,000. On looking at the order in council I find that the estimate for the two bridges, that is two bascule bridges, one over the 92582-1861
eastern entrance and the other over the western entrance to the harbour, is $800,000. One of those bridges is not now being asked for, and the western1 bascule bridge, as I understand the matter, would not cost any such amount as the $800,000 that has been mentioned. Those items may not be very material, but when my hon. friends opposite criticize the objections made to this bill and rather suggest that some hon. members on this side are objecting to this on the ground that it is wrong, I think they are not being quite fair to the committee. The fact is that whereas the estimate of the expenditure to be made by the government at that time was $6,400,000, the statement handed to me by the Minister of Public Works and read to the house last night shows that since that time the government have expended $9,542,459 in connection with the harbour of Toronto. Therefore it is quite apparent that the amount already paid is about one and a half times as much as the amount that was contemplated in the original order in council.
It is not the question of that difference that prompts me to take the objection that I have felt bound to take to this item. I realize how anxious members on both sides for that district are to have every expenditure possible made there, but there are many other districts that are not being given any expenditures at all at the present time. Further, as regards the airport which was given as the reason for building this tunnel, the plans of the airport as they appear at the present time seem to be dated at a time about April 25 and May 2, 1935, so that so far as the portion dated May 2 is concerned, the plans were made after this matter had been brought up in the house. We adjourned on April 17, so that those plans were prepared since this bill was introduced into the house with the suggestion that we should have only until six o'clock on the evening of April 18 in committee to consider whether the bill should go through as introduced.
Perhaps I have said everything that I can say in regard to the bill. I still feel at a time like this, that this is not the way in which public money should be spent. There are several other matters, as I and other hon. members on this side have intimated, upon which money could be more advantageously spent at the present time.
I do not know that I can add anything further; I do not want to take up more of the time of the committee, but I do think it my duty to direct attention to the fact that already about one and a half times the amount agreed upon, if you call the passing of the
Public Works Program

order in council an agreement-and I am not quarrelling particularly with that-has been spent.

speechtext: Then why mention it?

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: I mention it just to show my hon. friend that we are not bound by an agreement to go on and do this work, that there never was an agreement. There was an order in council; the amount contemplated in that order in council has been expended, and fifty per cent more than that amount has been spent up to the present time. I think that is a pretty complete answer to the agreement question. So far as the airport is concerned, that matter has been dealt with already. Of course no one contends that the airport was in contemplation when the order in council of 1913 was passed.

We are trying to
adhere to some extent to the particular clauses under discussion, and under those circumstances I do not want to go into these other matters. I would urge, however, that the housing needs of this country in cities like Toronto, Montreal, my own city of Winnipeg, and Vancouver are of very much greater importance than a matter of this character. In addition, the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Howden) pointed out that some of our cities have other very urgent needs. In my own city, for instance, there is the sewer scheme that is now hanging fire because of the difficulty of financing it. As I have listened to the discussion it has seemed to me that to provide a tunnel as part of a harbour scheme is stretching things just a little bit; it would seem as though this is a little aside from what we ordinarily consider to be definitely connected with harbour developments. I find a further difficulty in knowing whether we ought in any way to submit these matters to the city of Toronto or the authorities of that city. The Prime Minister has taken the stand that this federal government cannot deal with individual municipalities. If that

be the case, in this matter it is difficult for us to deal with any other body than the province of Ontario.
I think I should submit to the committee a telegram I have just received from the mayor of the city of Toronto which indicates the viewpoint at least of the civic authorities and which may help clarify the issue so far as that point is concerned. It is dated May 21, and reads as follows:
Anything less than the whole of the million dollars for a tunnel from Toronto's mainland to Hanlan's point of Toronto island will be regarded as discrimination against Toronto in the light of its needs and its importance, and opposition to this project does not represent views of majority of city council, board of trade and labour men generally. This fact should 'be made clear to the members of the House of Commons.
That is signed by Mayor James Simpson. I read this telegram, as indicating the point of view of the city of Toronto itself, but the telegram does not alter my view that whatever may be thought by the city of Toronto with regard to this particular expenditure of money, on the whole there are other ways in which the money could be expended at this time to very much greater advantage.

speechtext:
Does the former Minister of Public Works propose to make a Scrap of paper out of this agreement of 1913, under which the city of Toronto has spent about 88,000,000, the federal government $8,000,000, and the harbour commission some $28,600,000? I was in the office formerly occupied by the ex-minister when Mr. Rogers was Minister of Public Works, and at that time Mr. Rogers insisted that the work should go on under this agreement at once. He wanted the city to put a spade in the ground first, and we did so. He insisted on a new harbour, starting with the breakwater just beyond Queen's wharf, and that work has been completed with the exception of the work in connection with these two bridges. So I say this is a contract. As the hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Elliott) has said, it is true that a tunnel is not mentioned in that agreement, but two bridges to cost $400,000 each are, and at the present estimate one of these bridges will cost about $1,000,000; so it does not make any difference which is built, so far as cost is concerned. The cost of labour and material has gone up, and it is estimated that it will take in the neighbourhood of $1,000,000 to build one of these two bridges. In addition, a bridge is not a modern means of transportation in connection with waterways.

As a member from the city of Toronto, which has spent all this money in good faith, I feel it my duty to say something about what were nothing less than misstatements of fact. I do not wish to use that term, 'but I must say hon. gentlemen opposite did not know the facts. Yesterday it was stated that there were only two or three hundred people on the island, interested in this project. I wonder if hon. gentlemen opposite know how many people visit the island annually. Last year nearly two million passengers were carried to the island by the ferry boats. I should like to read two or three short sentences from the report concerning the operation of the ferries:
The island ferries, now owned by the city, were transferred to the management of the Toronto transportation commission in February, 1927. The fleet comprises six ferry boats and three freight craft, operating between the city mainland and the group of islands, part of the city, situated about two miles off shore. Ferry and freight service is provided between the mainland and three island points-Centre island, Hanlan's point and Ward's island. The oneway trip to any of these points is made in about fifteen minutes.
The ferry service was formerly operated by a private concern; then it became part of a system known as the Toronto Ferry Company. One of the principal directors of that company was Mt. Beatty, father of the president of the 'Canadian Pacific Railway, who was interested in this company from the time it was started. That company never made any money; it simply provided a service to the people of Toronto. I should like to say a word also with regard to some misstatements that have been made concerning Toronto harbour. In 1911 an act was passed relating to Toronto harbour. That was the constitution under which the harbour was developed, and I contend that Toronto harbour is purely a federal undertaking. The western entrance is owned by the government; the land covered by water is government property, and the eastern entrance is also owned by the government. Until recently even the life saving stations were government property. The turning basin at Ash-bridge's bay and all these points referred to in this bill are federal property as well. The Toronto harbour commission sends the Minister of Public Works and the Department of Marine the very same government reports that are sent by the other eighteen harbours under the control of this government.
The ferry service has become out of date; it is a relic of the ox cart days. There is a ferry boat called the Luella, taken off this spring which was built in 1880 and used to
Public Works Program
be the judges' boat in the days when there were boat races when Edward Hanlan rowed Wallace Ross of Halifax on Toronto bay for the single sculls championship of the world. I have before me the shipping list, and on the list I find the Trillium which, I believe, is their best boat, and which was built in 1910. The Bluebell was built in 1906, and the remainder are boats which are relics of the ox cart days.
I will tell you that the ferries cannot carry the crowd. It is a wonder to me there have not been some accidents. The two entrances to the harbour are under the control of the government; and some government docks are under the control of the government. The proposed tunnel will be the property of the parliament of Canada, the King represented by the Minister of Public Works. They will own the tunnel,-not the city of Toronto or the harbour commissioners, and they will place rights of user in it in the city and harbour board. It as proposed that the tunnel will cross the channel at the western entrance. All the property surrounding the entrance to Toronto harbour is under the control of the Department of Public Works and the Department of Marine and Fisheries. The harbour board has to make a return to the government. This tunnel when built, will cross a navigable stream, the western channel and would be subject to all federal harbour laws. It will come under the Navigable Waters Protection Act.
Last night an hon. member suggested the money should be spent on housing. May I remind the house that housing is receiving special attention, and that a discussion of a housing scheme is at this time out of order under the anticipation rule. I admit Canada up to the present time has done nothing with the problem of housing, and that proper housing is badly needed. Undoubtedly that condition applies in the city from which I come. I sat as a member of the committee investigating the housing problem. The statement was made last night that some of the million dollars must be spent in slum clearing. May I say that I do not know of any city which has done more to remove level crossings than has the city of Toronto. The city has spent $8,000,000 for the building of viaducts to eliminate level crossings along the waterfront. In the present year Toronto has in its estimates a vote of a million dollars to be spent in the elimination of level crossings. That sum wall be paid out of direct revenue or income and twenty per cent will be borne by and will come from the taxpayers of the city.
Public Works Program

Last evening one hon. member from Wellington spoke about St. John's ward. The condition in St. John's ward has been greatly improved. For the information of hon. members may I say that this particular ward is an old section of the city bounded by University avenue, Yonge street, Bloor street and Queen street. It comprises two-thirds of the district back of the city hall, running up to College street and including the new hospital, some buildings owned by the T. Eaton Company and some other large buildings. Two-thirds of that section has been cleaned out and only a small part remains to be improved.
Last evening I stated that the board of trade had passed a resolution endorsing the scheme. May I observe that I referred to the board of trade, and not to the council and board of control of the city. May I say to the hon. member for West Middlesex that I think the present harbour board were badly advised when they did not choose first to go before the city council, as I used to do when I was a harbour commissioner. In that way I informed the city council as to what we were going to do. No doubt a mistake was made when that was not done, and I hope it will not happen again. I must say however that the city council has not yet met to pass judgment on the building of the tunnel. It was almost unanimous in approving the erection of bridges, as were ratepayers' associations and other public bodies.
I can tell the committee why the bridges were not built; it was simply because the city and the harbour board wanted to have finished the $8,000,000 breakwater first from Bathurst street to the Humber. As chairman of the commission I attended a conference with the late minister, who gave us every assistance. Upon that occasion we asked to have the bridges included. I believe the hon. member for Parkdale was with me, and he will remember that we were told we would get one of these things. We were asked by some of the harbour people, and by some others to allow the matter to stand until the next year in order to obtain the necessary amount of money to finish the breakwater and the improvements at Sunny-side.
The city of Toronto has a large investment in Toronto island. It is not correct to state that only 200 or 300 people would be affected. I say there are more than a million people in the Toronto district interested in this matter; they are keenly interested in having the island used by more people all of the time rather than

by few people some of the time. Who are the 75 per cent of the island people whom the hon. member for West Middlesex described as being opposed to the building of the tunnel? Where do they come from? Are they ratepayers in the city of Toronto? I think he is referring to the two or three hundred people who live on the island and are opposed. There are at Ward's island about two hundred cottages. Centre island has lots of cottages, and Hanlon's island also forms a park larger than exhibition, park. The park at Centre island consists of 331 acres, and part of the remaining area is a lagoon. In addition to that, the city has millions of dollars invested in water service intake pipes, pumping stations, water tunnels, and a filtration plant on the island. There is a sick children's hospital established by the late John Ross Robertson, a man of great heart. This institution has been established on Toronto island to take care of the smaller children of that wonderful institution during the summer months. Then, in addition there is the Royal Canadian Yacht club and many other aquatic clubs. There is a regatta course, and the additional attraction of a Coney Island at Hanlan's point. These are places which attract great numbers of people during the summer months. Ten times more would go, however, were it not for the difficulty of reaching the island by ferry. If any hon. member would care to go down to the foot of Bay street next Friday, May 24, he would see women struggling with small children, trying to get off street cars. Then they would have a long walk to reach the ferry boat, and a long walk after they got off the ferries, and would have a long stop-over at Hanlan's point. If hon. members could see the discomfort and inconvenience these people are caused they would not oppose changing the plans from the building of a bridge to the building of a tunnel. If a tunnel were built street cars would go through, and in about three or four minutes passengers boarding the cars in the city could be taken to the western end of the island. Undoubtedly the original harbour scheme received support in 1911 because of the inclusion of the provision for the building of bridges so that people would be able to get to the island and use it.
Only a very small percentage of the people of Toronto visit the island. In the city there are about 700,000 people and another three or four hundred thousand in the immediate vicinity. Many more of those people would use the island, if it were more easily reached. In addition to that picnics would come from five or six townships nearest the city. The corporation owns the radials and the buses, and

Public Works Program
even at the present time picnics come to Toronto from points as distant as Hamilton and the section of the country north of that city. Even now some of them use the ferries to go to the island on a picnic, and I say that if we had the tunnel our buses and other forms of transportation would -be able to handle the crowds.
Last night we heard the hon. member for North York (Mr. Mulock). Something was said also about works for the general advantage of Canada. Some time ago we used to hear that the Newmarket canal would be a work for the general advantage of Canada. Now, if you please, the town of Newmarket has forgotten all about the general advantage of Canada and the celebrated canal. They have relegated those things to the ox cart days. Approaching the town of Newmarket on the main entrance to the town proper, we behold a sign in letters the size of that clock, and what do we see? We read nothing about the Newmarket canal or the general advantage of Canada. No,-what is on it? "Newmarket, the home of the Newmarket junior O.H.A. champion memo-rial cup holders (Dominion champions".) That is the advertising done by the town of Newmarket,-now, they do not even talk about the famous canal.
Then many other matters are mentioned as not being for the general advantage of Canada. The hon. member for Halifax had something to say about it last night. May I say he was in my riding of East Toronto, and I was glad to see him down there. In Toronto harbour we have several boats which came with cargoes from Halifax. I have before me an interesting harbour booklet which contains illustrations showing crowds of people at the island-not 200 people, as we have been told. Here we see an illustration of the lagoon, and here are a dozen war canoes in a race and regatta. We have an illustration of a Dominion day regatta with crowds three times the size of those attending the Canadian Henley, or the Canadian Canoe Association Annual regatta. This book has a picture of a boat from Halifax, the Moyra, unloading sugar in Toronto harbour. Look at these pictures of the ships in the harbour, and the elevators, and the oil tankers. The tonnage using Toronto harbour has gone up from 200,000 to nearly 3,000,000 tons. Look at all these new steamers and the development that has taken place all over the harbour. And the taxpayers of Toronto have paid S28,000,000 for these improvements. Toronto harbour is not like Montreal harbour or Quebec harbour, which do not pay their interest, but the taxpayers of Toronto have to pay for the upkeep of their harbour, and they have contributed the
annual deficits also. This book gives the history of the western entrance and of Toronto island. This western entrance was a work for the general advantage of Canada. It goes back to 1804 as set out in John Ross Robertson's Landmarks of Toronto, away back in the fifties and sixties. It goes back to 1804, and the war of 1812, when this western entrance stood right beside the old fort which was captured by the Americans in 1812. As I say, this book gives the history of the western entrance and of Toronto island. Toronto island is nothing but a huge sand bar acting as a breakwater to protect Toronto harbour.
My hon. friend from Shelbume-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) wants a bridge built to Sable island, where he says there are one hundred fishermen. I can tell him that Toronto is going to send some people down to represent Toronto at Halifax next summer. We are going to send down two or three "eights" from the Argonaut Rowing Club, and if my hon. friend is in the city of Halifax at that time these visitors from Toronto may be able to tell him what kind of a harbour we have. Our harbour is fifty per cent beautification and fifty per cent industrial development. My hon. friend has been more or less of a free trader. Does he want this bridge built to Sable island for one hundred fishermen according to the laws of supply and demand? The Liberal party in the maritime provinces has opposed subventions and bonuses and subsidies for coal, and very little coal was moved under their administration, but under the policy of the Conservative government 2,800,000 tons of coal has been moved to the head of the lakes. There are nearly 400,000 tons of coal to-day on boats in this ship channel shown in this book, as compared with 10,000 tons not so many years ago.
Here is shown Hanlan's Point where the old baseball park was, and as many as 150,000 people would go over there to watch the ball games, and to the three islands on a holiday, going across the bay on the old ferries.
So far as this tunnel project is concerned, let me say that the city of Toronto has done nothing but pay, pay, pay all the time. We have a life-saving station which has cost the city taxpayers nearly 880,000 a year with equipment, and we provide a life-saving service for the whole of lake Ontario, for the Georgian bay district, and the Muskoka district. Whenever an accident happens on the water they phone for Toronto's life-saving equipment, and it is sent all over the province at no cost to this government at all.
The hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rin-fret) says that Toronto -harbour cannot be compared with Montreal habour. Of course

speechtext: I should like to ask the minister one or two questions. How long will it take to complete the proposed tunnel? How much work will be done in 1935 and will the work be carried out under the supervision of the Department of Public Works?

speechtext:
I will answer the questions in the reverse order to which they have been put. Upon a review of the history of this proposition it will be found that the matter was presented to council through the Department of Public Works. Any work which has been done in Toronto harbour by the dominion government has been done through that department. This bill contains a provision, to which I referred last night, that any work to be done under it will be assigned by the governor in council to such department as is thought -best under the circumstances. In view of the history of this project, one would expect that the Department of Public Works will be in charge. I hope so as that department is familiar with everything which has been done. As to when the work will be completed, that will depend upon the terms of the contract. The preparation of plans and specifications will not be difficult and I would think that a very substantial- part of the work could be done
Public Works Program

during 1935. This work is not seasonal and could be carried on through the winter. I cannot speak definitely as to how much work will be completed during 1935, but it should be a substantial part.
There were one or two other matters which were mentioned. The former Minister of Public Works (Mr. El'liott) gave an estimate of the cost of these two bridges. The amount he stated is the amount in the order in council but he should remember that that was passed back in 1912 or 1913. As he knows, the cost of construction has almost doubled since that time, so that while the estimates were probably correct at that time they are not applicable to the present day. My hon. friend is correct in saying that there was no formal agreement but the effect of the provisions of the order in council is to make it an agreement. The order in council provides what each is to do and gives further details. There is no time specified during which the work shall be done. My hon. friend referred to certain work which had been done since but the terms of the agreement are not specific and the fact that an agreement was made with regard to certain developments does not prevent a contribution being made by the dominion government toward the construction of other works.

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
The hon. member for
East Toronto (Mr. Church) made a remark with regard to what I had an opportunity of saying last night respecting assistance in providing facilities for connecting the mainland of Nova Scotia with Cape Sable island. I want to correct the hon. gentleman's geography. I was not talking about Sable island but about Cape Sable island, which is a very different place. I was speaking about the possibility of helping to provide communication across the sheet of water known as Barrington passage to Cape Sable island, where there are, not one hundred fishermen as my hon. friend suggests but between three and four hundred, and where the dealers live who serve that whole area in the collection of fish and the sale of it in foreign and Canadian markets. Apparently my hon. friend did not get the gist of what I was trying to propose, but I suggested that work under this particular act should be work which, if possible, should make people self-dependent, and provide needed facilities for better transportation between the mainland and Cape Sable island, on which there is the thriving town of Clark's Harbour, with a population of a thousand or twelve hundred citizens; and a surrounding community of probably eight hundred more. I suggested

that if we are providing relief works we could well help to provide communication between the mainland and that island so as to enable these people to get their product off to market under proper conditions and at cheaper cost than are possible under the present system. In doing that, it seemed to me, we should be helping people to help themselves; we should be providing employment in connection with the work to be done. It seems to me that such a facility would assist these people in earning a living. Now I am not in the slightest measure setting up Nova Scotia as against Toronto; I am simply comparing the benefits of the work I suggest in connection with Cape Sable island with what my hon. friend has said regarding the benefits which would result from the Toronto project. The hon. gentleman said quite plainly that this tunnel is for the purpose of providing communication between the city of Toronto and this holiday place, this picnic place, this summer place, whatever it may be-and I do not use these terms in any offensive or facetious sense- where people, may enjoy themselves. He said that the purpose was to provide such communication so that people might get to the island cheaply and easily. Now that is not helping people to make a living; it is merely helping them to enjoy themselves. It is providing cheaper transportation, I grant. But if we attempt out of the dominion treasury to provide for cheaper transportation to the people in the different cities on their tramways or in connection with their ferries or their bus services, then it strikes me that whatever funds we may have at our disposal will soon be exhausted. I am trying to impress on the committee and on my hon. friend from Toronto the fact that such is not the object of the sort of expenditures which are being made under this bill. We could find many places where we could contribute towards the people's comfort and happiness and at the same time fail to carry out the principle of this special public works legislation. These public works are being built as relief works, to provide employment, and in the second place they are being built for useful purposes to produce revenue and to assist people in making a living. But this tunnel does not fulfil that second requisite. My hon. friend is quite frank when he says that we do not realize the possibilities to all the people of Toronto which this tunnel will afford. Let me tell him that we do realize them; but we submit with deference that there are many other projects which will better carry out the objects of legislation of this kind.

Public Works Program
My hon. friend has based his contention on the ground that a promise was made. I submit to this committee that if for twenty-two years our friends on the other side have permitted their consciences to be so elastic that they did not feel called upon to fulfil this promise, then they might at least leave the matter another year or more and feel that they are not wounding their moral sensibilities very much. No one I have heard has answered the strong point that has been made, that this matter has been allowed to stand for twenty-two years. If it could stand for that length of time why can we not wait another year until financial conditions are better? But apart from that the former Minister of Public Works has pointed out that, if we are talking about promises, the promise or understanding or undertaking set out in that order in council was that the dominion government should spend $6,400,000. That undertaking, according to the figures given by my hon. friend, has been more than carried out.

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: They were to spend that amount on certain specific projects.

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
My hon. friend points out that it was for certain specific projects; but whether it was for certain specific projects or not, the government has spent, as a matter of fact, not $6,400,000 but over $9,000,000 in connection with works relating to the harbour of Toronto. So that I do not think it behooves anyone to throw it in our faces that we are repudiating our obligations to the city of Toronto or the Toronto harbour commission when we have spent nearly fifty per cent more than the amount involved in the original order in council. I really feel that that is the weakest ground on which the Minister of Public Works could possibly base his case, because no one can justify rushing in in 1935 to implement a promise that has been allowed to lie dormant for twenty-two years. As I have pointed out there are promises made by my hon. friends opposite which need to be implemented much more urgently than this old promise. There was the promise of old age pensions to Nova Scotia-one hundred per cent was to be paid. For the last five years Nova Scotia has been paying twenty-five per cent which the Prime Minister promised in 1930 would be paid by the dominion. Why not fulfil that promise, if the treasury is full enough to be able to provide for these other things. Then there is the Halifax-Dartmouth bridge, which was promised in the 1925 election. I remember
that celebrated circular, "Vote for Black and Quinn and get the Dartmouth bridge," or something to that effect. Why not fulfil that promise? And without extending the record, there are a good many promises made by my hon. friends which are more urgent than this twenty-two year old one, and I repeat that the obligations of the dominion under that order in council were fairly well carried out by the expenditure of over $9,000,000 instead of the $6,400,000 mentioned in the order in council. I remind you also, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member for Toronto gave us the real reason why the bridge was not built. He said it was because the harbour commission would rather have the money spent in extending the breakwater. But now the Minister of Public Works proposes that although as desired by the commission we spent the money in connection with the breakwater instead of the bridge we should now provide twice the cost of the bridge by building a tunnel. As the former Minister of Public Works points out, the bridge would have cost $400,000. The present Minister of Public Works thinks that is below the amount it would cost to-day in view of the difference in the value of money. Public Works Program

I think the people affected will appreciate the proper expenditure of the money, but whether it will have any particular effect on the major coming event that is in our minds just now is another question. The experience of past years, especially of the provincial elections of last year, would seem to show that large expenditures made for no particular purpose except to throw money around have not had a very desirable result so far as the government has been concerned, so I am warning my hon. friend not to expect too much in a political way from these expenditures.
